title: Learn by Doing: Methods
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then every past question on methods and overloading, each with its model answer, and the method taught from nothing.
intro: Part A is the objective questions on this topic. Part B is past questions only. Both papers open on this topic: 25/26 asks you to define overloading and the role of the signature, and 24/25 asks for three definitions and then a program that overloads area.

lockin.big: "The signature is the name and the parameter list. The return type is not part of it, which is why two methods cannot differ by return type alone."
lockin.sub: Java passes by value: a method cannot change the caller's int. An array variable holds a reference, so its contents can be changed.

methodFrames.teach:
A method is a named block that does one job. The header carries four things in order: modifiers, return type, name, parameter list.

public class Area {    static double area(double r) { return Math.PI * r * r; }    static double area(double l, double w) { return l * w; }    static double area(double b, double h, boolean triangle) { return 0.5 * b * h; }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.printf("circle %.2f%n", area(7));        System.out.printf("rectangle %.2f%n", area(4, 5));        System.out.printf("triangle %.2f%n", area(6, 8, true));    }}
Outputcircle 153.94
rectangle 20.00
triangle 24.00
methodFrames.ask: Which of those four make up the SIGNATURE, the part the compiler uses to tell two methods apart?

methodFrames.check: The name and the parameter list.
methodFrames.teach:
The name and the parameter list, and nothing else. The return type is NOT part of the signature, which is the precise point 25/26 asks for: it is the signature that lets the compiler resolve an overloaded call at compile time.

So overloading is several methods with the same name whose parameter lists differ in number, type or order.
methodFrames.ask: Two methods differ only in return type, int and double. Will that compile?

methodFrames.check: No: same signature, so it will not compile.
methodFrames.teach:
No. The signatures are identical, so the compiler cannot choose, and it is a compile error. That single sentence answers half the overloading questions in the objective half.

Now the distinction the paper asks for in words: a parameter is the name in the header, an argument is the value in the call.
methodFrames.ask: A void method and a value returning one. What is the difference in what the CALL is worth?

methodFrames.check: A void call is not a value; a value returning call is.
methodFrames.teach:
A void method hands nothing back, so its call cannot be assigned or printed. A value returning method ends in return, and its call IS a value. In the exam, prefer a method that returns: Section B and C both say "a method that returns".

public class PassByValue {    static void change(int n, int[] nums) {        n = 99;        nums[0] = 99;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        int n = 1;        int[] nums = {1, 2, 3};        change(n, nums);        System.out.println(n + " " + nums[0]);    }}
Output1 99
methodFrames.ask: Now pass by value. What does this print, and why does the array behave differently from the int?

methodFrames.teach: 1 and 99. Java always passes by value, but the value of an array variable is a REFERENCE to the array. The copy of that reference still points at the same array, so a change through it is visible to the caller; the copy of the int is just a copy.
methodFrames.ask: Last: static. Why can main call a method directly only if that method is static?

methodFrames.check: main is static, so it has no object to call an instance method on.
methodFrames.teach: Because main is static, so it runs without an object, and it can only call other static methods directly. A non static method needs an object first: new Thing().method(). Marking a helper method static in an exam program is the simplest way to keep it callable from main.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question One, 2 marks

scenario.text: [2 Marks]A. Define method overloading in Java, and state precisely the role that the method signature plays in enabling the compiler to resolve an overloaded call at compile time.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
GivenNothing. Recall.
Asked forTwo things joined by "and": a definition, then the mechanism. "State precisely the role" is asking how the compiler decides, not what overloading is.
The marks2 marks: one for the definition, one for the mechanism. Answering only the first half caps you at one.
WatchThe word "at compile time" is the hinge. Overloading is resolved statically, by signature; overriding is resolved at run time. Say "compile time" out loud in your answer.

exam.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 2 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Q1 a · define method overloading, and the role of the signature · 2 MARKS

Model answer.

Method overloading is a feature that allows a class to have more than one method with the same name but different parameter lists (differing in the number, types, or order of parameters).

The method signature is a method's name together with its parameter list. Its role in resolution is this: at a call such as add(2, 3), the compiler compares the number, types and order of the arguments written at the call site against the parameter list of every candidate with that name, and selects the one whose signature matches (widening the argument types if no exact match exists). Because the resolution uses only what appears at the call site, and the return type is not part of the signature, the return type plays no role: two methods differing only by return type are rejected by the compiler as a duplicate definition. The choice is therefore made entirely at compile time, which is why overloading is called compile-time (static) polymorphism.

Where the marks are: one for the definition, one for "signature = name + parameter list" and the fact that the return type is excluded. Saying "the compiler picks the right one" without saying how is half an answer. See Units 5.1 and 5.6.

exam.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 3 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Q1 a · define method signature, overloading, and void method · 3 MARKS

Model answer. One mark each, and each is one sentence.

  1. Method signature. A method's name together with its parameter list (the number, types and order of its parameters). The return type is not part of the signature. It is what the compiler uses to tell one method from another.
  2. Method overloading. Declaring more than one method with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class, so the compiler chooses between them at compile time by matching the arguments at the call site against each signature.
  3. Void method. A method declared void, meaning it returns no value. It is called as a statement on its own, cannot be used in an expression, and may use a bare return; to exit early.

Where the marks are: the examiner asked for signature and overloading in the same breath deliberately, because the second is defined by the first. Say "signature = name + parameter list, return type excluded" and the overloading definition writes itself. Units 5.1, 5.2 and 5.6.

exam.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 3 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Q1 b · debug squarecalc · 3 MARKS
Compiler outputerror: <identifier> expected

The errors, listed. The question says list and correct, so list them: a correction with no list is half an answer.

  1. Line 2: main(String[] ) has no parameter name. A parameter needs a type and a name. Fix: main(String[] args).
  2. Line 4: no semicolon after double result = square(num).
  3. Line 8: square(int) has no parameter name. Fix: square(int n).
  4. Line 9: n does not exist. It is the symptom of error 3: name the parameter and n exists. Worth saying out loud in your answer, because it shows you understand the cause rather than listing every red squiggle.
  5. The braces are missing for both square and the class.

Three marks, five errors. Do not stop at three: the marker is looking for the set, and errors 3 and 4 are one fault with two faces.

Code · q1 b corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class SquareCalc {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int num = 5;        double result = square(num);        System.out.println("Square is: " + result);    }    public static int square(int n) {        return n * n;    }}
OutputSquare is: 25.0

Look hard at that output: 25.0, not 25. square returns an int, and 25 is stored into a double result. Java widens the int to a double on the way in (Unit 5.7), so what gets printed is a double, and a double always prints its point. Nothing is wrong; but if you wrote "Square is: 25" you have missed a mark that costs nothing to get right.

questions.heading: 2024/2025, Question One, 7.5 marks

scenario.text:
[7.5 marks]D. Write a program that overloads a method named area to compute:

i.    The area of a circle

ii.   The area of a rectangle

iii.  The area of a triangle.

Call these methods and print out their values in the main method.

questions.asked: Shape: Write a program. A full program, marked on structure as much as on logic. The two papers set this shape 17 times between them, 1 of them on this topic.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
GivenNothing. You write the whole program.
Asked forThree methods that share the name area and differ in parameter list, plus a main that calls them and prints.
The marks7.5 marks. The last sentence is a separate instruction carrying its own marks: three correct methods with no main is an incomplete answer.
WatchOverloading is resolved by the parameter list. Circle takes one argument, rectangle and triangle take two, so rectangle and triangle collide unless you distinguish them. Decide how before you start writing.
Taught inUnits 5.6 and 5.7.

exam.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 7.5 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Q1 d · overload area for circle, rectangle and triangle · 7.5 MARKS
Must memorise · The obvious answer to this question does not compile

Circle needs one number. Rectangle needs two. Triangle needs two.

So rectangle is area(double, double), and triangle (base and height) is also area(double, double).

That is the same signature. It will not compile.

Overloading needs different parameter lists, and "base, height" is not different from "length, width": the parameter names are not part of the signature, only the types (Q1 A, which you just answered). Write both and javac says:

error: method area(double,double) is already defined in class

The resolution: give the triangle a three-number formula, so its signature is area(double, double, double) and distinct. Heron's formula takes the three sides:

s = (a + b + c) / 2     and     area = √ s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) 

MEMORY HOOK: overloads differ by types, not by names. If two of your methods take the same types in the same order, you have one method and a compiler error.

This is the single most valuable thing in Question One, and the examiner may not have noticed it. Say it explicitly in your answer: "base and height would collide with length and width, so the triangle is done by Heron's formula on three sides, giving a distinct signature." That sentence proves you understand overloading, which is what the question is for.

Code · q1 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class AreaOverload {    // i. circle: one number, so the signature is area(double)    public static double area(double radius) {        return Math.PI * radius * radius;    }    // ii. rectangle: two numbers, so the signature is area(double, double)    public static double area(double length, double width) {        return length * width;    }    // iii. triangle: base and height would ALSO be area(double, double), which is    // the rectangle's signature and will not compile. Three sides gives a distinct    // signature and a genuine formula: Heron's.    public static double area(double sideA, double sideB, double sideC) {        double s = (sideA + sideB + sideC) / 2;        return Math.sqrt(s * (s - sideA) * (s - sideB) * (s - sideC));    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("Circle, radius 7      : " + area(7.0));        System.out.println("Rectangle, 5 by 3     : " + area(5.0, 3.0));        System.out.println("Triangle, sides 3 4 5 : " + area(3.0, 4.0, 5.0));    }}
OutputCircle, radius 7      : 153.93804002589985
Rectangle, 5 by 3     : 15.0
Triangle, sides 3 4 5 : 6.0

Check the triangle without trusting Heron. 3, 4, 5 is a right triangle, so its area must be half of 3 × 4, which is 6. Heron gave exactly 6.0. When you use a formula you cannot see through, feed it a case whose answer you already know. Math.PI and Math.sqrt are Unit 3.6.
